I think this is down to how investors think about how to value a piece of a company. I think about it almost the same way as I think about sports gambling.

There's a value proposition in which direction the stock is going to go and how long it's going to take to get there. It only makes sense to be invested in a stock if you think it's going to be worth more later than it is now and the amount of time your money is tied up in this stock is commensurate with the profit you may get as a result.

Investors work on limited information about companies, and having a track record can influence a buying decision one way or another. It may matter to some investors and not to others. For many, it's weighed against the price of the stock. Would you bet $100 on a company with a short track record? What about $10,000, $100,000, or more? Generally there's a point where people drop out of buying more of a stock and say that they can't justify the risk given the information they have. That's the expected value that Anthropic will receive from that investor.

Anthropic needs to worry about what that number is for a huge amount of individual investors and how to maximize the amount of money put into the cost of their stocks, and there's very little chance that they can attract the biggest pool of investor money without some of those people considering their longevity vs a more established company like Meta. It may not matter to all investors, but the fact that it will matter to some makes it a factor in the total valuation.

There are a few points I'd like to make here.

First, the frontier is jagged. There are errors that Qwen3.8 Flash Next make that Opus 5.5 doesn't make, but the reverese is also true: Opus 5.5 makes errors that Qwen3.8 Flash Next doesn't make. The latter will likely be fewer, but they won't be zero. Outside of really large differences in capabilities, there is no total ordering among models, only a partial one.

As an aside, do you always run Opus 5.5 at max reasoning in order to minimize errors, too? I suggest most people don't, because they have their own intuition for good enough vs. cost.

Second, Opus 5.5's strength are autonomous tasks. For interactive, HITL work, it's not a particularly great choice. This includes its preferring complex Bash commands over tool use and inscrutable Python scripts, but also often not even explaining what it does. It is not a great choice to use as a virtual pair programmer, because following along what it does and maintaining a mental model is harder than with some other models (though probably because of benchmarks that prioritize autonomous work, these and related problems have infected other models, too). You can address that to an extent with CLAUDE.md instructions, but even that has imperfect results.

Finally, if you rely on a model not to make mistakes in order to ensure correctness, your software development process is fundamentally broken. You need to assume that any model will make at least some errors and need a development process that accounts for that. The problem here is not necessarily which model creates fewer errors, but which model creates code where errors are easier to discover. Ironically, more powerful models may create more complex code, making that harder.

You can see an analogous effect with reasoning effort in FrontierBench 2.0 [1]:

"FrontierCode is one of the few coding benchmarks where writing additional (correct) code doesn’t necessarily raise a model’s score. This leads to an interesting phenomenon: models can score lower at higher reasoning effort. Because this non-monotonicity often matches user sentiment but is hard to see in other evals, we consider it a useful feature of the benchmark."

A example:

"This task comes from PostHog’s open-source Android SDK, which apps use to record analytics events. When the device is offline, the SDK writes events to disk and sends them the next time the app starts. The task is to fix a startup bug in which two modules send data at the same time: the live queue sends new events while a legacy integration, PostHogSendCachedEventsIntegration.kt, sends the cached ones. The two race, and events reach the server out of order.

"At low effort, GPT-6 Astra moves cache loading into PostHogQueue.kt, removes the sending logic from the legacy integration, and leaves the SDK’s public API untouched, which produces a passing solution.

"At max effort, the model often deletes PostHogSendCachedEventsIntegration.kt outright and spreads its responsibilities across other legacy files. This also fixes the race and passes most of the hidden behavior tests. But the deleted class is part of the SDK’s public posthog.api surface, so removing it introduces an unnecessary breaking change for every app that references it. Scope blockers, which deterministically check that the model hasn’t modified certain files, catch this change, and the agent fails the task."

[1] https://cognition.com/blog/frontier-code-2.0

Here's a stress test of sorts that I've had it working on the last couple of days: We have a C -> microcode compiler written in C (most of that was work done 'back' in the Opus 4.6/4.8 era). I gave it the docs for that compiler and asked it to implement it in OCaml (since it's not very common, but also is a good implementation language for compilers). It can use the first compiler as a golden to compare against. It's essentially: C language parser -> AST -> IR -> [optimization passes] -> microcode (+ some verilog code). It's basically at the point now where the original compiler has been. Not only does this generate microcode it also has to generate some Verilog code that loads and runs the microcode as well as run simulations in Verilator to confirm functionality. I asked it to come up with some new optimizations that the original compiler doesn't have and it came up with a couple that in some cases reduce microcode lines by up to 30% (less microcode in this machine means more performant). These are ideas that Claude didn't come up with when it was working on the original compiler back in the 4.6/4.8 era(and I recall prompting it several times asking it if there might be other optimizations we could perform).

So all in all, I put it at Opus 4.8 level, at least. And in some ways it's exceeding 4.8.

> People with something to lose tend to actively "vote" only on what they know something about.

"Prediction" markets have rendered this clearly false of late.

> the reason I trust the market is the "skin in the game"

The market expects economic bailouts and other assistance during downturns, because individual investors with 401(k)s demand it, despite the perversions of market incentives that result.

To be more precise, the reason I trust the market is the "skin in the game" and the decentralization / localization of decision making. People with something to lose tend to actively "vote" only on what they know something about.

Not that it's somehow "not people" (of course it is).
The market is a group of people, and much of that decision making is in the hands of a very small proportion of it.

I don't trust the market to calibrate "value" the same way that I subjectively define it.

But I trust the market to calibrate value about 10,000x more than I trust any person or group of people to do so. The thought of that is frankly terrifying.

children.author: NortySpock
children.text:
I think also the demand for software tokens is going to be bursty, and many things are going to be one-time software ports.

- Nervous about Redis being written in C? Switch to Garnet.

- Bun ported from Zig to Rust for $165,000 at API pricing -> https://bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust

- Microsoft ports Copilot runtime to Rust for $120,000 in API costs without blocking other development work -> https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/generative-ai/migrating-the-gi...

- Someone made a "clean room port" of Total Annihilation in golang, looks like it started in August and is now the most convenient way to play Total Annihilation. https://github.com/nanolathe-gg/nanolathe

- You only have to decompile / reverse engineer an existing game once and now you can have an agent occasionally add features.

Once you do the port and have worked out the regression issues, assuming you are switching to a safer language with better guarantees, you are now off of the old codebase and don't have to pay the costs of the old codebase. It's just a one time burst of token usage.

Costs of tokens will continue to fall as more hardware either becomes rentable (datacenter comes online) or moves into the used market, as workloads move onto users individual machine (because smaller models are becoming more capable and getting better inference engines and harnesses).

You can also task an agent with researching for "list the top 5 performance improvements we might be able to make" and have it research overnight, then the next day start a fleet of agents iterating through the findings that seem the most workable . Once you gain the performance win, that's basically permanent.

I think that token usage is a very elastic market, you can choose to spin up a fleet of agents or... you can stay human-in-the-loop, or you can type code yourself if you don't have a token budget.

So, yeah, I don't think Anthropic or OpenAI are worth much when hot on their heels are open-weight models hosted by major cloud providers + Nvidia and cloud providers themselves building their own models.
